title: Binary Lifting and Ancestor Queries
summary: Precomputed 2^k-ancestor tables for O(log n) kth-ancestor and LCA queries on a static tree — the technique for answering thousands of ancestor queries fast.

slides.markdown:
The LCA algorithms from the previous topic are O(h) per query — fine for a handful of queries, but if a tree is queried **thousands of times** and never changes shape, paying O(h) per query adds up. Binary lifting trades a one-time O(n log n) preprocessing cost for O(log n) per query afterward, which wins decisively once query count is large relative to tree size.

The core idea: precompute, for every node, its 2⁰-th ancestor (parent), 2¹-th ancestor (grandparent), 2²-th ancestor, and so on — a small table per node — then answer any "kth ancestor" or LCA query by composing powers of two, the same way any number decomposes into a sum of powers of two in binary representation.

slides.subTitle: Precompute 2^k-th ancestors, then compose powers of two
slides.markdown:
Instead of storing every node's ancestor at every possible distance (which would be O(n) per node, O(n²) total), store only ancestors at **power-of-two distances**: 1 hop up, 2 hops up, 4 hops up, 8 hops up, and so on, up to roughly log₂(n) different distances per node.

Any distance k can be reached by combining a subset of these powers of two — exactly k's binary representation. To find the ancestor 13 hops up (13 = 8 + 4 + 1 in binary), jump 8 hops, then 4 hops, then 1 hop from wherever that lands — three jumps total instead of thirteen individual parent-pointer hops, because each jump covers an exponentially larger distance.

slides.subTitle: With a DP over (node, k)
By decomposing k into its binary representation
slides.markdown:
```python
def kth_ancestor(node, k):
    for i in range(LOG):
        if k & (1 << i):       # is bit i set in k's binary representation?
            node = up[i][node]
            if node == -1:      # ran off the top of the tree
                return -1
    return node
```

Each set bit in k's binary representation corresponds to one jump using that power-of-two column — for k = 13 (binary `1101`), this jumps 8, then 4, then 1 (skipping the 2-column, since that bit is 0), landing exactly 13 hops up in three table lookups. O(log n) per query, after the one-time O(n log n) table build.

slides.subTitle: Lift the deeper node first, then binary-search the split point
slides.markdown:
LCA using binary lifting has two phases. First, **equalize depths**: if one node is deeper than the other, lift it up (using the kth-ancestor query) until both nodes are at the same depth — now they're guaranteed to reach any common ancestor, including the LCA, after the same number of further steps.

Second, with both nodes at equal depth, lift **both simultaneously** by decreasing powers of two, but only when doing so keeps them at **different** nodes — this is effectively binary-searching for the largest jump that doesn't overshoot past the LCA. Once no jump of any size can be taken without making them equal, their immediate shared parent is the LCA — one more `up[0]` lookup on either node.

slides.sectionTitle: LCA query using the precomputed table
slides.subTitle: In O(log n) per query
slides.markdown:
```python
def lca(u, v, depth):
    if depth[u] < depth[v]:
        u, v = v, u
    diff = depth[u] - depth[v]
    u = kth_ancestor(u, diff)  # equalize depths
    if u == v:
        return u
    for i in range(LOG - 1, -1, -1):  # binary search from largest jump down
        if up[i][u] != up[i][v]:      # only jump if it doesn't overshoot past the LCA
            u, v = up[i][u], up[i][v]
    return up[0][u]  # one final step reaches the actual LCA
```

O(log n) per query, matching the kth-ancestor query's complexity — a dramatic improvement over the O(h) general-tree LCA when the tree is large, static, and queried many times.

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting to equalize depths before lifting both nodes
Binary lifting vs Euler tour + sparse-table RMQ
slides.subTitle: Both O(log n) LCA, different constants and use cases
slides.markdown:
| | Binary lifting | Euler tour + sparse-table RMQ |
|---|---|---|
| Query time | O(log n) | O(1) (with sparse table) |
| Preprocessing | O(n log n) | O(n log n) |
| Also answers kth-ancestor | yes, directly | not directly — a separate structure |
| Conceptual complexity | moderate | higher — needs Euler tour + RMQ machinery |

Both are legitimate O(n log n)-preprocessing answers to "many LCA queries on a static tree," but they're not identical: the Euler-tour approach can answer LCA in true O(1) per query (using a sparse table for range-minimum-query on the tour's depth sequence), strictly better than binary lifting's O(log n) — at the cost of more machinery to set up and maintain. Binary lifting is usually the better default when kth-ancestor queries are also needed, since it answers those directly without extra structure.

slides.sectionTitle: When binary lifting earns its preprocessing cost
slides.subTitle: Many queries on a static or append-only tree
slides.markdown:
Binary lifting's O(n log n) preprocessing is wasted effort if the tree is queried only once or twice — the plain O(h) LCA from the previous topic is simpler to implement and asymptotically fine for a handful of queries. The crossover happens specifically when query count Q is large enough that Q × O(h) exceeds the one-time O(n log n) setup cost plus Q × O(log n) — which, for a reasonably balanced tree, is almost always true once Q is more than a small constant.

This is a direct instance of the amortization reasoning that shows up throughout this curriculum: pay a larger fixed cost once, in exchange for a cheaper cost per subsequent operation — worth it exactly when "subsequent operation" happens often enough. Binary lifting also requires the tree's shape to stay fixed (or only grow, in some variants) between the preprocessing step and the queries — a tree with frequent structural edits invalidates the table and needs re-preprocessing, which erases the whole benefit.
